I was playing around with words today, imagining a conversation taking place between a parent and a child. The parent wants to help the child know they are safe, that they are loved. The child is afraid.
“I love you.”
“Do you trust me?”
“Yes, I believe in you.”
“Are you safe? Are you at peace?”
The conversation continues. The words are simple, but they are not easy. Parent and child both have to trust the words, to work through a relationship with them.
If we believe that words are important, that they have the power to create, sustain and transform, we need to give them careful thought. An apology can be mimed with a bowed head. A hand on a shoulder can say “I’m sorry.” A gesture, glance or good deed can replace a word that is not essential. Sometimes we need to think beyond the words. How do we know how much we are loved? How do we know that our words are believed?

The thoughts, conversations and writings of Khalil Gibran have been influential in my life and work. I first read The Prophet when I was a teenager. I didn’t understand the story, but some of the words and images stuck with me. As a young adult, I read The Madman, Gibran’s first book in English, published in 1918 by Alfred A. Knopf. I was impressed by the strength of Gibran’s vision and ability to articulate it.
My favorite book of Gibran’s is The Garden of the Prophet, published posthumously in 1933. The story takes place in the city of Orphalese, where the prophet Al Mustafa has lived for 12 years. He is about to board a ship that will carry him home. A group of people gather and discuss life and the human condition with him. They ask him questions and he gives them answers. The first question is, “Who are you, Ocean of love?”
I’m not interested in the answers as much as I am in the questions. The questions the people of Orphalese ask are all inspired by Gibran’s challenge to ask what we are afraid to say. Gibran’s questions are about love, marriage, children, giving, eating and drinking, work, joy and sorrow, houses, clothes, buying and selling, crime and punishment, laws, freedom, reason and passion, pain, self-knowledge, teaching, friendship, talking, time, good and evil, prayer, pleasure, beauty, religion, and death.
The questions Gibran asks are the essential questions. Gibran’s challenge to me is to ask those questions, and then to trust the answers I find.

Nonverbal communication, sometimes referred to as body language, is the nonverbal signals that a person displays while communicating. In addition to the use of words, nonverbal cues make up a large part of human communication. When the verbal and nonverbal messages match, people feel more at ease. If the nonverbal cues contradict the verbal messages, people feel more tense and less comfortable. Effective and meaningful communication about emotions requires the words, tone of voice, and facial expression to support each other, i.e. be "congruent". A person's posture, eyes, and hands can tell a story on their own that doesn't match their words. When the posture, eyes, and hands tell the same story as the words, people relax and believe the speaker. The role of body language in human communication.
When nonverbal cues match the words, people feel more relaxed and open. When the nonverbal cues contradict the words, people feel more tense and less comfortable.
Body language includes facial expressions, body posture, gestures, eye movement, touch, and the use of space. Body language can be used to tell a person how you are feeling, such as smiling when you are happy or crossed arms when you are upset. It can also be used to express an idea or show what you are doing. Body language can keep your real intentions from being lost in translation. You must be aware of how you act and what your body language is saying. While many of the meanings of body language are universal, there are some variances across cultures, countries, and religions.

In 1967, Albert Mehrabian published a paper on the importance of body language in human communication. In that paper, he said that 55% of communication happens through body language, 38% through the tone of voice, and 7% through words. His findings were based on research in a very controlled setting, specifically where a person listens to a single word and forms an impression about the attitude of the speaker. It is not a good indication of the amount of information that is transmitted by body language, which is much more complex.
The figures 55% and 38% refer to Mehrabian's studies on the communication of feelings and attitudes, not of information. The original study is about a person's ability to decode two conflicting messages, a verbal message (such as the words "maybe") and a nonverbal message (such as "don't count on it"). It is one of the most commonly used indicators of the economic health of a country, and it is frequently associated with economic and social progress. GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced in a period, within a country. It is the standard measure for measuring economic growth. Put simply, GDP is the sum of all the things a nation produces, and the nation's income. GDP is often used as an indicator of the economic health of a country, as it is generally closely correlated with other measures of economic and social welfare.

However, many critics have pointed out that GDP is not intended to be used as a measure of economic or social performance, and that the use of GDP to measure such things has contributed to what is known as "the growth imperative", which is a policy focus on growing the economy, or keeping the rate of growth of GDP stable. Critics have pointed out that GDP does not take into account the societal, environmental, or even economic costs of growth. Hence, by using GDP as a measure of economic progress, an economy that is growing while producing a declining standard of living, and while having adverse impacts on the environment, will be considered to be doing "well".

Hence, it is more important to the overall well-being of a country to keep a steady growth rate than to aim for the highest GDP growth rate possible.

Iodine is essential in the synthesis of thyroid hormones, which play an important role in regulating growth, mental development, and overall metabolic rate. In the United States, salt is iodized to prevent this deficiency. However, iodine deficiency is common in many areas of the world, especially in mountainous regions and in countries located at a large distance from the sea. In these countries, iodine often needs to be supplemented in other ways, such as in the soil and in the water.
Iodine deficiency in humans can cause severe medical conditions, including hypothyroidism, goiter, and neurological symptoms. These symptoms are often evident in fetuses and young infants, and the effects can be permanent. The lack of iodine in animals is also a major issue: for example, iodine deficiency in cattle causes excess thyroid hormone levels in the animals and impairs their growth rate.

A stock market bubble (sometimes referred to simply as an asset bubble or a speculative bubble) is the rapid escalation of asset prices based on unjustified exuberance. The result is an increase in real estate prices and the stock market. Bubbles can last for years until the price suddenly plummets. The market crash of 1929 is the classic example of a bubble and burst, but there have been many others since.
Investors often pool their money into a single investment, and when a bubble bursts, people lose money or their investments become worthless.
The term “bubble” in reference to financial crisis originated in the British South Sea Bubble of 1711–1720, so-called because the South Sea was the principal stock being traded.
The Dutch tulip mania of the 1630’s is considered the world’s first recorded speculative bubble; it has been used as a cautionary tale against financial speculation ever since. The Mississippi Scheme in France and the South Sea bubble in England were two famous early stock market bubbles.
The Roaring Twenties stock market bubble (which caused the Great Depression) and the United States housing bubble (which caused the Great Recession) are examples of debt bubbles. A bubble forms when the price of an asset rises far beyond what its underlying value can justify. This can be caused by a number of factors, including media speculation, the bias of analysts who may have a personal interest in inflating the asset’s value, and the human instinct to follow the crowd.
The “mechanism” that is used to explain the development of bubbles is a positive feedback loop. When the price of an asset rises, people notice and are inclined to buy some of that asset themselves, in the hope that the prices will continue to rise and they can make a profit. This demand drives prices up further, which leads to more people buying.

The results are in the pre-print bioRxiv, so they haven’t yet been reviewed by experts in the field.
Gaucher’s disease is a common lysosomal storage disorder named after French physician Philippe Gaucher, who described it in 1882. It’s the most common type of lysosomal storage disease. Lysosomes are sacs of enzymes within cells that digest large molecules and pass fragments to other parts of the cell for recycling. When the lysosome doesn’t function normally, excess products destined for breakdown and recycling are stored in the cell. Lysosomal storage diseases (LSDs) are a group of over 70 rare inherited metabolic disorders. The biochemical basis of the disease was elucidated in the 1960’s by Roscoe Brady. A hereditary deficiency of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase (also called glucosylceramidase), which acts on glucocerebroside, causes Gaucher’s disease. Glucocerebroside is a sphingolipid, which are known to participate in inflammation and apoptosis. When the enzyme doesn’t work properly, the lipid builds up inside cells, particularly in white blood cells and especially in macrophages (mononuclear leukocytes). Macrophages that clear these cells cannot eliminate the waste product, which accumulates in fibrils and turns the macrophages into ‘Gaucher cells.’ The early signs of Gaucher’s disease are anemia, low blood platelet count, swelling of the liver and spleen, and a low white blood cell count.
Gaucher’s disease has three common clinical subtypes. Type I (non-neuropathic) is the most common and least severe. It has some residual enzyme activity, accounting for the lack of neuropathology in this type. About 80 known GBA gene mutations are grouped into three main types. Type I, II, and III. Type II (acute infantile neuropathic) typically begins within 6 months of birth. Symptoms include enlarged liver and spleen, extensive progressive brain damage, eye movement disorders, spasticity, seizures, limb rigidity, and poor ability to suck and swallow. Type II symptoms are progressive and the children usually die by age two. People with type III (chronic neuropathic) can begin to show symptoms at any time in childhood or in adulthood. This type progresses more slowly than the others. It has slowly progressive neurologic symptoms that are milder than type II. Other symptoms are the same as those in type I, but usually more severe. Neuronal damage associated with the disease was discovered in the 1920’s. The exact mechanism of neurotoxicity is not understood, but is thought to involve a reaction to glucosylsphingosine.
Mutations in the glucocerebrosidase gene cause Gaucher’s disease. A person has to inherit two copies of the defective gene to have type I, II, or III Gaucher’s disease. If they only have one copy, they’re considered a carrier. About 10 percent of the Ashkenazi Jewish population are carriers of Gaucher’s disease.
